hints: Look carefully at the right-hand side of the graph above 50 °C. Which curve stays higher, free papain or immobilised papain?
Remember what a fall in activity at high temperature means. It shows denaturation, so holding activity higher means resisting denaturation better.
walkthrough:
**Read what the graph is really showing**

Look at the x-axis (temperature) and y-axis (activity of papain). Up to about 40 °C both forms have the same high activity.

Above about 50 °C, both curves fall, but the immobilised papain curve stays above the free papain curve.

**Link the fall to denaturation**

At high temperatures, hydrogen and ionic bonds break. The tertiary structure unfolds and the active site loses its shape.

That is denaturation, and we see it as a loss of activity. A slower loss means the enzyme is more resistant to heat.

**Decide what immobilisation does**

Because immobilised papain keeps more activity at 60 to 80 °C, it is less easily denatured.

In other words, trapping it in alginate beads increases its stability at higher temperatures.

options.A: Immobilisation helps preserve the active site shape, it does not alter it. The higher activity shows the shape is maintained better.
options.B: The graph shows the opposite. At higher temperatures the immobilised enzyme has higher activity than the free enzyme.
options.C: Correct. Immobilised papain retains more activity above 50 °C, showing it is more stable and more resistant to heat denaturation.
options.D: Immobilisation can reduce collisions, but this graph shows increased activity at high temperature, so this does not explain the result.
